extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating enablement, utility, best mode, and use of prior art in U.S. patent examination (35 U.S.C. 101, 112 and related practice). Explains examiner burdens, applicant rebuttal, and when to make rejections under utility and enablement provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing prior art documents (commercial availability and sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial availability of an identified prior art computer system is very pertinent to the issue of enablement, but merely citing excerpts from technical publications/affidavits is not sufficient unless it is made clear that a person skilled in the art would know which parts of the cited circuits could be used or how they could be interconnected to act in combination to produce the required results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits that merely cite excerpts without showing which parts apply or how to interconnect components are insufficient (In re Forman). Where circuits are essentially standard components of an identified prior art system and a standard device attached thereto, the analysis may be less critical. Examiner should ensure cited prior-art systems are actually commercially available if relied upon for enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art patents/publications must predate the effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art patents and patent application publications relied on to show the state of the art for enablement must have a publication date earlier than the effective filing date of the application under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents issued after the filing date of the application under examination are not evidence of subject matter known to persons skilled in the art because their subject matter may have been known only to the patentees and the PTO (In re Budnick; In re Gunn). Examiners must check dates when relying on patents/publications for enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing prior patents does not by itself demonstrate integration or enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely citing prior art patents to show that challenged components are old may not suffice to show how those components would be interconnected to function in the claimed complex combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must set forth the integration of the prior art; otherwise undue experimentation or more than routine experimentation may be required to implement the claimed invention (In re Scarbrough). Any cited patents used to show components are old must be analyzed for germane relevance and whether they provide better disclosure than applicant's own disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability of programming techniques for demonstrating known techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent or publication cited to show that a particular programming technique is well-known does not demonstrate that one of ordinary skill could make disclosed programming techniques unless the known and disclosed techniques are of approximately the same degree of complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should assess whether the cited programming technique and the applicant's disclosed technique are comparable in complexity (In re Knowlton). If not, the citation may not support enablement of the programming aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments of counsel cannot substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of counsel may be effective in showing examiner error, but arguments alone cannot take the place of evidence in the record once an examiner has advanced a reasonable basis for questioning the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the record consists substantially of arguments and opinions of applicant’s attorney, courts have indicated that factual affidavits could have provided important evidence on enablement (In re Budnick; In re Schulze; In re Cole; In re Knowlton; In re Wiseman). Examiners should require evidence rather than accept counsel argument as sole support when a reasonable factual basis for rejection has been presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between utility (35 U.S.C. 101) and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101) requires some specific, substantial, and credible use; 35 U.S.C. 112(a) requires disclosure of how the invention can be used — i.e., how the required use can be carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are different legal requirements and rejections under them should be imposed separately. A showing that an invention has utility does not by itself prove compliance with enablement if undue experimentation would be needed to practice the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: When utility is not satisfied (nonuseful or inoperative claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim fails the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101 because it is nonuseful or inoperative, it necessarily fails the how-to-use aspect of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should make both rejections (35 U.S.C. 112(a) and 35 U.S.C. 101) where subject matter has been shown to be nonuseful or inoperative (In re Fouche). Do not impose or maintain a 112(a) rejection grounded on 'lack of utility' unless a proper 101 rejection exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden to show lack of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner concludes an application claims an invention that is nonuseful, inoperative, or contradicts known scientific principles, the burden is on the examiner to provide a reasonable basis to support this conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of challenging an asserted utility: they must provide evidence showing that one of ordinary skill would reasonably doubt the asserted utility. Only then does the burden shift to the applicant to rebut (In re Fisher; In re Swartz; In re Brana; In re Bundy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant rebuttal standard for asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner has made a prima facie showing that utility is doubtful, the burden shifts to the applicant to provide rebuttal evidence sufficient to convince one of ordinary skill in the art of the invention's asserted utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no predetermined amount or character of evidence required; it varies with the claim and whether the asserted utility contravenes established principles. Applicant's evidence need only make the asserted utility 'more likely than not' true (Ex parte Ferguson; In re Gazave; In re Chilowsky; In re Irons). See MPEP § 2107.02 for more on evaluating evidence related to utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement can fail even when utility is satisfied
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may have a specific and substantial utility and a credible basis for that utility, yet still fail the enablement requirement if a person skilled in the art would need to engage in undue experimentation to practice the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases, no 101 rejection is appropriate but a 112(a) rejection should be made (Mowry v. Whitney). Examiners must separately consider enablement even when utility is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement evaluated against the full scope of the claims (commensurate in scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter. The focus is whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled; the examiner must determine exactly what is encompassed by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination looks to the claim as a whole (including dependent claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(d)/pre-AIA 112, fourth paragraph). If a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement across that range (AK Steel v. Sollac). The examiner should identify the subject matter considered enabled if making a lack-of-enablement rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must teach how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without 'undue experimentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not everything necessary need be disclosed — well-known information may be omitted. The required scope of enablement must have a reasonable correlation to the scope of the claims (In re Wright; In re Buchner; In re Fisher). Examiners should consider the level of ordinary skill in the art and what is routine knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection under 112(a) for breadth not 112(b) definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection that the claim is broader than the enabling disclosure is an enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and not a definiteness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are not rejected as broader than the enabling disclosure simply for omitting limitations that are presumed within ordinary skill. One looks to the specification to find out how to practice the claimed invention (W.L. Gore; In re Johnson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are to be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification; the teachings of the specification must not be ignored when analyzing enabled scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation in light of the specification does not mean everything in the specification is read into the claims (Raytheon v. Roper). If a reasonable interpretation of a claim is broader than the description in the specification, the examiner must ensure the full claim scope is enabled. Limitations and examples in the specification do not generally limit what is covered by the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single means claim vulnerability to enablement rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A single means claim (a means-plus-function recitation that is not in combination with another recited element of means) is subject to an enablement rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) if it covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated purpose while the specification discloses at most only those means known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Hyatt: single means claims that cover every conceivable means for a result when spec discloses limited means can be nonenabling. Similar issues arise when claims depend on a recited property that could cover all structures achieving that property while the spec discloses only inventor-known structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative subject matter standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render a claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which conceived-but-not-yet-made embodiments would be inoperative or operative with expenditure of no more effort than is normally required in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophetic examples do not make a disclosure nonenabling (Atlas Powder). A single inoperative embodiment among many operable ones may not render the claim nonenabled (In re Angstadt). However, claims that read on significant numbers of inoperative embodiments may be nonenabled where the specification fails to clearly identify operative embodiments and undue experimentation is required (Atlas Powder; In re Cook).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical feature taught in specification must be claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: A feature that the specification teaches as 'critical' and is not recited in the claims should result in a rejection of such claim under the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of criticality considers the entire disclosure; features merely described as preferred are not 'critical' (In re Mayhew; In re Goffe). An enablement rejection based on omission of a disclosed critical limitation should be made only when the specification language makes clear that the limitation is critical for the invention to function as intended. Broad language in the disclosure tends to rebut arguments of criticality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement (statutory obligation and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention (pre-AIA language preserved in 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for examination purposes). Determining compliance requires a two-prong inquiry: (1) whether the inventor possessed a best mode at filing (subjective), and (2) whether the written description disclosed the best mode sufficiently to enable one skilled in the art to practice it (objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best mode requirement prevents applicants from retaining their best-known way while disclosing only second-best embodiments (In re Nelson). Failure to disclose the best mode can be found even absent active concealment if the inventor knew of a specific material or method that would make reproduction possible but did not disclose it (Union Carbide v. Borg-Warner). The best mode requirement is distinct from enablement: best mode imposes an obligation to disclose the inventor's recognized best practice; enablement looks to whether the public can practice the claimed subject matter generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode practice after the AIA and related examiner considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the AIA amended 35 U.S.C. 282 to make failure to disclose best mode not a basis to invalidate or render claims unenforceable in a litigation, examiners should continue current examination practice for best mode compliance in applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 15 of the AIA modified the treatment of best mode in post-issuance proceedings but did not eliminate the requirement for examination purposes. If an earlier-filed application’s filing date is actually necessary, examiners should consult supervisors if it appears the earlier application does not disclose the best mode for carrying out a claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode — considerations and limitations (examples and practical rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical considerations: determine what the invention is (defined by the claims); a specific example is not required; designation of an embodiment as 'best' is not required; updating best mode is not required in priority filings; best mode defects cannot be cured by adding new matter after filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not set forth details unrelated to the essence of the invention (In re Bosy). Presence or absence of a working example is not dispositive (In re Gay; In re Honn). There is no statutory duty to label an embodiment as 'best.' Do not add best mode by amendment (new matter) — such amendments should be objected to and treated as new matter (In re Hay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner presumptions and proof standard for best mode rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume best mode is disclosed unless evidence shows otherwise. A best mode rejection is proper only where (A) the inventor at filing knew of a mode better than others and (B) the disclosure is inadequate to enable one of ordinary skill to practice that best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first component is subjective and requires evidence that the inventor had superior information at filing; absent such evidence, do not proceed to the second component. The second component is objective: assess whether the specification enables practice of the best mode. Best mode rejections in ex parte prosecution are extremely rare because necessary evidence often is not available (Chemcast approach). Only evidence of concealment (intentional or accidental) that shows disclosure quality is so poor as to effect concealment should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of best mode evidence and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Case examples illustrate when best mode was satisfied or not: known computer program withheld but specification sufficient; failure to disclose a commercial motor not concealment where similar motors widely available; omission of routine-known ways does not imply concealment absent intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent (In re Sherwood; Honeywell v. Diamond; W.L. Gore & Assoc.; High Concrete Structures) to guide fact-specific determinations. Evidence must tend to show concealment — mere nondisclosure of routine or widely available items is often insufficient to support best mode rejection.
